title: Writing for Belafonte and keeping the score transparent
summary: Jones explains overwriting for television, using two or three elements, Rimsky-Korsakov and Duke's comment of too many notes.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: You said -- you're quoted in the inaudible book as saying that when you were writing for Harry Belafonte, that you approached your writing there as Duke did, for sound effects rather than the notes.
Do you want to expand on that?

Well, I'll tell you. With Harry I had to make a 180 degree turn, because he had been like Calypso, and then writing for television, and the idea was to overwrite, because it's easier to take out than to have to write it in the studio.
You know, you can always -- see, one of the basic things I think in writing, if you look at your manuscript, you always have -- well, all you need is two or

three elements and you have to keep them going. They can just be expanded and be larger. You have your rhythm section working, you have your soloists working, and that's two elements right there. And then you have the orchestra working. Now, if it gets too busy it sounds like scrambled eggs, you know?
So if the -- the main thing was to keep it transparent.

Like I used to study Rimsky-Korsakoff's book on orchestrating, and I think he was one of the greatest in keeping it transparent, where you can understand it all, you know? And to learn, don't be afraid of simplicity, you know?

Because, well, when you go through the early age you think you want to prove something, and oh, there are some things I've written before, years ago, that I won't even play, you know, because as you go along you get the experience on playbacks and hearing them back. Well, with Harry I learned that, and Duke used to always say -- he'd tell some writers -- he never did bother me at all. I think he liked the way I wrote. He'd say, 'Too many notes,' you know?
And he was right. You know, as you go

along and become seasoned, you begin to realize just write only what's logical. Like in having a conversation, if you write only what's logical, you just go -- well, you have to communicate with the ear, the ear of the public, or the people that are not participating in our field, so make it so they understand it, and pretty soon you'll enjoy it more yourself.
